prompt: Which statement correctly describes the simple model of viscous drag force acting on an object moving through a fluid?
options: The drag force is constant at all speeds.
The drag force is non-zero when the object is stationary.
The drag force is zero when stationary and increases as speed increases.
The drag force acts in the same direction as the velocity of the object.

answer.explanation: Option 3 is correct. In the simple model of fluid drag, the drag force is zero when the object is stationary relative to the fluid, and increases monotonically as the relative speed increases.

distractor_explanations: Option 1 confuses fluid drag with solid kinetic friction, which is approximately constant over normal speeds.
Option 2 confuses fluid drag with solid static friction, which can exert a holding force at zero speed.
Option 3 correctly describes the zero-speed condition and monotonic speed dependence of fluid drag.
Option 4 incorrectly claims drag acts with velocity; drag always opposes relative motion.
hints: Consider whether a stationary object experiences fluid drag in still air.
How does air resistance change when you ride a bicycle faster?
solution: In fluids, drag force is zero when stationary and increases as speed increases, always opposing relative velocity.
teacher_walkthrough: Drag arises from collisions with fluid particles and viscous shearing.
When speed is zero, no collisions occur preferentially from any direction, so D = 0.
As speed increases, more fluid particles are encountered per second with greater momentum transfer, so D increases.
